nodes.question: How many distinct test runs were conducted, and what were their DEET concentrations?
nodes.answer: Three distinct test runs were conducted with DEET concentrations of T1 (5 mg/L), T2 (10 mg/L), and T3 (25 mg/L).
nodes.paragraph: Two distinct experimental runs were conducted to evaluate removal potential: control runs (without DEET) and test runs (with DEET). The test runs included T1 (5 mg/L), T2 (10 mg/L), and T3 (25 mg/L), all performed in a 250- mL Erlenmeyer flask containing 100 mL of BG-11 algal medium inoculated with Chlorella vulgaris during the growth phase. experimental configuration. nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What is the typical concentration range of DEET in insect repellent products?
nodes.answer: The concentration of DEET in products typically ranges between 5 and 99%.
nodes.paragraph: T1 conditions resulted in more significant lipid formation than other test runs, making biofuel for DEET-contaminated wastewater a feasible alternative. Keywords Chlorella vulgaris, DEET, Acute toxicity, Biochemical composition, Removal Introduction N,N-Diethyl-m-toluamide (DEET) is the main ingredi - ent used in products such as lotions, sprays, and mate - rials (towelettes and roll-ons) as insect repellent. DEET is very effective in deterring the biting of arthropods (mosquitoes and ticks). A third of American adults use DEET to protect themselves from mosquito-borne ill - nesses such as malaria, zika virus, Lyme disease, spotted fever, and the Nile virus [1, 2]. The DEET concentration in the products typically ranges between 5 and 99%, and it is approved for skin applications, not for ingestion, and is not employed in food-related contexts [3]. DEET functions by impeding the olfactory perception of these hematophagous insects toward the human scent. Follow - ing its initial development by the United States Army in 1946, DEET was subsequently licensed for civilian use in 1957 [4].
